title: Heart of Darkness
description: Marlow's night journey up an African river to find the ivory agent Kurtz: the central European text about empire, and one of the great English novellas. It is a prose fiction work of 1899 by Joseph Conrad; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under novel of consciousness and the stream of mind; ghost story and the modern weird tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Marlow, a riverboat captain, sits on the deck of the Nellie on the Thames and tells the story of a journey up the Congo to fetch Kurtz, the company's most successful agent, who has installed himself as a god among the local people and has gone mad. Marlow finds him dying and hears his last words — 'The horror! The horror!' — and returns to Europe carrying his memory.
narrative_structure: Three-part serial narrative framed by Marlow's narration aboard the Nellie; a journey structure with a descent into the interior.
principal_characters: Charles Marlow; Mr Kurtz; the Intended; the Manager; the Harlequin; the Accountant
literary_form: Novella (three-part serial, Blackwood's Magazine 1899; book form in Youth, 1902)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
historical_context: The Congo Free State of Leopold II, where Conrad himself served as a river captain in 1890 and saw the rubber and ivory system at first hand; the book appeared in the year of the Boer War, at the height of the imperial confidence it dismantles.
literary_significance: Heart of Darkness is the indispensable European text about empire and one of the founding works of modern fiction: it invented the colonial journey narrative that the century would find endless uses for, gave the language 'the horror', and its technique — the framed narrator, the delayed disclosure, the symbolic river — made Marlow the model for the modern unreliable narrator. Chinua Achebe's attack on it in 1977 made it the centre of the debate about the colonial canon, which is itself part of its record.

plot_or_argument: Jim, the chief mate of the Patna, jumps from the ship with the officers when it seems certain to sink with 800 pilgrims aboard; the ship does not sink, and Jim is publicly disgraced at the inquiry. He moves from port to port, and finally to Patusan, a remote Malayan settlement, where he becomes 'Tuan Jim' and the trusted ruler of the people — until the pirate Gentleman Brown's raid and the death of Dain Waris destroy him, and he goes to his death willingly.
narrative_structure: Non-linear retrospective narration: Marlow's oral account framed by a third-person narrator, with letters and reports inserted.
principal_characters: Jim; Charles Marlow; Captain Brierly; Doramin; Dain Waris; Jewel; Gentleman Brown
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
historical_context: The age of sail's last years and the Malay Archipelago of the 1880s; the code of the sea, the merchant marine inquiry and the imperial adventurer. Conrad's own experience as a master mariner and his reading of the East gave the novel its exact detail.
literary_significance: Lord Jim is Conrad's greatest novel and one of the finest studies of moral failure in English: it made 'one of us' a permanent phrase, invented the technique of the multiple retrospective narration (Marlow collecting Jim's story from others), and gave the twentieth-century novel its central subject — the man who fails his own code and cannot be forgiven. title: Nostromo: A Tale of the Seaboard

It is a prose fiction work of 1904 by Joseph Conrad; it belongs to The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method and it is catalogued here under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: In the fictional South American republic of Costaguana, Charles Gould inherits the San Tomé silver mine and devotes his life to making it productive. When a revolution threatens, the silver is sent to sea with Nostromo, the Italian foreman of the dockers, who is trusted by everyone; he saves the silver, hides it, and is slowly destroyed by the secret of it, while the mine's wealth corrupts the whole society around him and the country passes from one dictator to another.
narrative_structure: Five-part structure moving backward and forward in time, with a large cast whose lives intersect around the mine and the silver.
principal_characters: Nostromo; Charles Gould; Emilia Gould; Martin Decoud; Dr Monygham; Antonia Avellanos; Don José Avellanos

historical_context: The Central American and South American republics of the late nineteenth century, their cycles of revolution and foreign debt, and the imperial economics of the silver mine — Conrad drew on his knowledge of the Latin American revolutions and on the history of the American-financed mines.
literary_significance: Nostromo is the greatest political novel in English of the period: it invented the fictional republic as a model of the whole of politics, its structure of parallel and intersecting lives over decades is one of the most ambitious in the novel, and its analysis of how wealth and foreign capital corrupt every revolutionary ideal has never been surpassed.

title: The Secret Agent: A Simple Tale
description: A Soho shopkeeper in the pay of a foreign embassy plots a bomb attack on Greenwich Observatory, and destroys his own family in the process. It is a prose fiction work of 1907 by Joseph Conrad; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under detective novel and the golden age mystery; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Mr Verloc, a lazy Soho shopkeeper who sells pornography and frequents anarchist meetings, is an agent of a foreign embassy. Ordered to stage an outrage against 'the fetish of science', he sends his simple-minded brother-in-law Stevie to carry a bomb to Greenwich; Stevie stumbles and is blown to pieces, and Verloc's wife Winnie, discovering the truth, murders him and is herself destroyed. The novel ends in a fogbound London of police, spies and solitary misery.
narrative_structure: Chronological narrative with a delayed revelation of the murder and a documentary account of London's police and anarchist underworld.
principal_characters: Mr Verloc; Winnie Verloc; Stevie; Adolf Verloc's mother; Chief Inspector Heat; the Assistant Commissioner; Vladimir; Ossipon
literary_form: Novel; detective novel, first issued in 1907
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the fair-play mystery: the puzzle is stated in plain narrative prose, the clues are given to the reader as they are given to the investigator, the timetable and the plan are exact, and the solution is delivered in a set-piece explanation. The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
historical_context: The anarchist scare and the spy mania of the 1890s, the Greenwich Observatory bombing of 1894 (an actual attempt by a French anarchist), and the London of Soho, the embassy and the detective police. The record dates the work as composed between 1906 and 1907 and first published in 1907 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; The Golden Age of Detective Fiction, it is catalogued under detective novel and the golden age mystery; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
literary_significance: The Secret Agent is the greatest English novel about terrorism and one of the darkest comedies in the language: it invented the domestic spy novel, has never been equalled in its analysis of the political agent as an ordinary, lazy, frightened man, and the murder of Stevie is one of the most shocking scenes in English fiction.

title: Under Western Eyes
description: The political novel of Russian autocracy and exile: a student informer in St Petersburg and Geneva, and the impossibility of innocence under a police state. plot_or_argument: Razumov, a St Petersburg student, is approached by a fellow student, Haldin, who has just assassinated a government minister and asks for help; Razumov betrays him to the police and is set to spy on the revolutionary exiles in Geneva. There he falls in love with Haldin's sister Nathalie and is slowly destroyed by guilt, finally confessing to the revolutionaries and being deafened and crippled by their vengeance.
narrative_structure: First-person narrative by an English teacher of languages, with Razumov's diary embedded in it; two unequal parts (Russia, Geneva).
principal_characters: Kirylo Sidorovitch Razumov; Victor Haldin; Nathalie Haldin; Peter Ivanovitch; Sophia Antonovna; Councillor Mikulin

The author's characteristic manner is the framed narrative and the shifting narrator (Marlow).
historical_context: The Russian autocracy of the 1900s, the Okhrana, the revolutionary emigration in Geneva and the assassination of the Minister of the Interior Vyacheslav von Plehve (1904); Conrad drew on his Polish family's experience of Russian exile.
literary_significance: Under Western Eyes is the finest English novel about the police state and the moral condition of the informer: it is the direct ancestor of Koestler's Darkness at Noon and Orwell's Nineteen Eighty-Four, and its portrait of Razumov is one of the great studies of betrayal and self-knowledge in the language.

title: Tono-Bungay
description: The rise and fall of a patent-medicine fortune and a portrait of England from the 1870s to the 1900s — Wells's finest novel. It is a prose fiction work of 1909 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

George's other life as an aeronautical engineer and his flight over Africa give the novel its images of the modern age; the book ends with the uncle ruined and dying and England seen as a system of shams.

The record dates the work as composed between 1908 and 1909 and first published in 1909 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.

title: The Outline of History: Being a Plain History of Life and Mankind
alternative_titles: Outline of History: Being a Plain History of Life and Mankind
description: The whole history of life and mankind in one narrative: the most widely read history book ever written in English, and the foundation of the modern popular history. It is a prose work of 1920 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under documentary prose and the reportage book; critical essay and the modern review and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Wells begins with the formation of the earth, traces the evolution of life, the emergence of the human species, the ancient civilisations, the world religions, the empires, the Renaissance, the Enlightenment, the industrial revolution and the First World War, and closes with an argument for a world state as the only alternative to self-destruction.
narrative_structure: Chronological world survey in forty chapters, from cosmology to the League of Nations. It was issued in instalments, and each part carries its own set piece and its suspended close. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The work was issued in serial parts, and the instalment shapes the chapter. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
historical_context: The First World War and the peace settlement, the collapse of the old empires, the League of Nations, and the new mass readership created by cheap printing and the book clubs — the book sold over two million copies in the 1920s.
literary_significance: The Outline of History made history a popular literary form: it sold in millions, created the modern illustrated popular history, and its argument for a single world civilisation made Wells the most influential public intellectual of the period. It is the book that taught the twentieth century its own past.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as H. G. Wells. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Cassell in two volumes in November 1919 and in a one-volume Definitive Edition in 1920; the full title is The Outline of History: Being a Plain History of Life and Mankind. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Shape of Things to Come: The Ultimate Revolution
alternative_titles: The Shape of Things to Come
Shape of Things to Come: The Ultimate Revolution
description: A history of the next two centuries: the collapse of civilisation in a world war, the rise of a technocratic world state, and the flight to the moon. It is a prose fiction work of 1933 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia and it is catalogued here under scientific romance and the utopian tale; dystopian fiction and the anti-utopian satire and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Written as a manuscript by a diplomat of the future, the book narrates a world war beginning in 1940 that destroys civilisation, a plague, a long dark age, the emergence of a technological ruling order, its unification of the world, and the launching of the first lunar expedition — ending with the question of whether humanity will choose the stars or stagnation.
narrative_structure: Future history narrated as a recovered manuscript with a framing preface and footnotes. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel cast as the document, diary or confession of a subject inside the system, the invented vocabulary of the state carrying the satire.
principal_characters: Dr Philip Raven; the World Council; the Modern State
literary_form: Future history (based on the film Things to Come, 1936)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the rapid, transparent narrative built for a mass readership.
historical_context: The rise of fascism, the bomber and the fear of total war, the technocratic and utopian movements of the 1930s, and the new medium of the film (Korda's Things to Come, scripted by Wells, appeared in 1936).
literary_significance: The Shape of Things to Come is Wells's last great utopian statement and the most influential future history of the 1930s: it anticipates the world war, the bombing of cities, the plague and the world state, and its images passed directly into the cinema and into the political imagination of the period.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1933, as future history (based on the film things to come, 1936), by Herbert George Wells. Composed between 1931 and 1933. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The History of Mr Polly
description: A small draper burns down his own shop, fakes his death and discovers freedom on the road. It is a prose fiction work of 1910 by Herbert George Wells; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Alfred Polly, a quarrelsome, incompetent draper in Fishbourne, is trapped in an unhappy marriage and a failing business. He resolves on suicide, but before he can act the shop catches fire; he takes the opportunity to disappear, is presumed dead, and reinvents himself as an inn-keeper and woodsman, fighting a local bully, finding a companion, and finally returning to visit his widow's new marriage.

The record dates the work as composed between 1909 and 1910 and first published in 1910 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama; comedy of manners and the drawing-room stage.

title: The Old Wives' Tale (Bennett, 1908)
description: The lives of two sisters in the Potteries, from the 1860s to the 1900s: the great English novel of time and provincial endurance. plot_or_argument: Constance and Sophia Baines grow up in their parents' drapery shop in Bursley. Constance marries the shop's manager and stays in the town; Sophia elopes to Paris with a commercial traveller, is abandoned, and becomes the proprietress of a Paris boarding house. The novel follows them for forty years, through the siege of Paris, the deaths of their parents and husbands, and old age, ending with Constance's death and Sophia's return to the town.
narrative_structure: Four-part chronicle moving chronologically across two generations and two countries. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
principal_characters: Constance Baines; Sophia Baines; John Baines; Samuel Povey; Gerald Scales; Chirac; Mr Critchlow
meter_and_prosody: Prose. historical_context: The Potteries of the 1860s–1900s, the Franco-Prussian War and the siege of Paris (1870–71), the drapery trade and the chapel culture of the Five Towns. The record dates the work as composed between 1907 and 1908 and first published in 1908 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England, it is catalogued under condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.

title: Clayhanger
description: A printer's son in the Potteries struggles against his father and the provincial world, in the finest English novel of the autodidact. title: The Man of Property

When Irene falls in love with the architect, young Philip Bosinney, Soames sues him for the cost of the house; the lawsuit destroys Bosinney, and Irene leaves Soames. title: Howards End
